claims.text: The baseline eutectic high-entropy alloy has a dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
Internal boundaries in the lamellar colonies act as microcrack-initiation sites during room-temperature tensile loading.
Ti is a microalloying element known to promote grain-boundary cohesion.
An addition of approximately 0.5 at% Ti will segregate to lamellar-colony interfaces during solidification and subsequent processing.
Targeted Ti segregation will enhance cohesion at lamellar-colony interfaces.
Strengthened internal interfaces reduce local stress concentrations.
Reduced interfacial stress concentration delays microcrack nucleation during tensile deformation.
Interfacial Ti segregation will delay microcrack propagation.
Ti present at the interfaces will contribute to load bearing and thereby increase yield strength.
Adding approximately 0.5 at% Ti will simultaneously increase yield strength and room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the unmodified alloy.
The microalloyed alloy will exhibit fewer and more propagation-resistant interfacial cracks than the baseline.
Conventional eutectic HEAs commonly face a trade-off between high strength and tensile ductility.
The baseline's limited tensile ductility is caused by interfacial brittleness.
The proposed benefit is confined to dual-phase lamellar eutectic HEAs under room-temperature tensile deformation.
The optimum microalloy concentration and element depend on the host-alloy composition and processing history.
Analogous grain-boundary engineering in other alloy systems supports the proposed segregation-and-cohesion mechanism.
